content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/ingest-book

# Ingest Book

Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.

**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.

## Model split (cost vs quality)

This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
  doesn't compound across the book.

## Schema for every entry note

Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.

```yaml
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: <domain-slug>
book: <book-slug>
chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
topic: <2-5 word topic>
category: [tag, tag]
confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <Human title of the idea>

**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
**Example** — one concrete instance.
```

**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.

## Phase 1 — Intake

1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.

`_book.md` template:
```markdown
---
type: book-index
book: <book-slug>
title: <full title>
author: <author>
domain: <domain-slug>
ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <title> — ingest map

| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|--------|---------|
| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
```

## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)

**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
  confidence entries from a scanned file.
- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`, where A and B are
  0-based PDF indexes and the range is inclusive: `--pages 12-20` returns 9 pages). Each page
  comes back with `page` (0-based index) and `viewer_page` (what a PDF viewer shows, index + 1).
  Cite pages one way throughout a book and state the convention in `_book.md`. For each:
  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.

**Kindle highlights:**
- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".

**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
  confidence ≤ untested.

## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)

- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.

## Phase 4 — Close-out

1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
   if an advisor exists.
4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.

## Rules
- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.

# Flint ingest plan: getting Drive into Flint over time

Status: draft for Eric's review, 2026-10-13. Read with `docs/PLAN.md` (phases) and `docs/QUEUE.md` (named books and their order). This file adds the parts those do not cover: how the Drive grows, how much each step costs, who approves what, and how sub-agents are used.

## 1. The problem

Eric's Drive is large and still growing. The Sept 29 manifest counted 62,072 files (544 GB). After removing duplicates, 29,750 files (229 GB) are unique. Most are video (7,266 files, 151 GB) or papers and books (9,493 files, 28 GB). Only a small share can be read in full by an agent. The plan has to decide what to read, what to only index, and what to skip, and it has to keep doing that as new files arrive.

**Numbers conflict.** The Oct 12 build plan cites 17,847 files, 11,644 unique and 187 GB. The Sept 29 manifest says 62,072, 29,750 and 229 GB. A fresh recount is the first task (step 0 below). No budget in this plan should be treated as final until that count is done.

## 2. Principles

1. **Tier before you read.** Every file gets one of three tiers. Only Tier A gets the full review gate.
   - **A, deep ingest:** a paper, book or deck that will be cited. Full gate.
   - **B, catalog only:** indexed by title and metadata, searchable, never atomized.
   - **C, skip:** not useful to Flint (logistics, duplicates, forms, personal files).
2. **Gate what gets cited.** Nothing reaches the vault without the review gate in `docs/PLAN.md` and the AGENTS.md conventions. The gate is expensive, so it runs only on Tier A.
3. **Small batches, approved in short sittings.** Eric approves candidates in batches of at most 10. Approval is the only human step that cannot be automated.
4. **Model tier by job.** Deterministic code for catalog, dedup and text extraction (no tokens). Haiku for triage and labelling. Opus for atomizing and reviewing. Never Haiku for atomizing (ingest-book rule).
5. **Never ingest athlete data.** DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult exports and PFF exports stay out of the catalog. W13 stays held. This rule is checked at catalog time, at compile time and in any test set.
6. **Drive is the source of truth. The repo holds only pointers and summaries.** Source PDFs and video never go into git (AGENTS.md: files over 95 MB never go in git).

## 3. The pipeline

| Stage | What happens | Who or what | Cost | Exit criterion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Catalog (monthly) | Walk Drive roots, record new and changed files since the last manifest, dedup by md5 | `scripts/build_manifest.ps1` (Windows) or Mac equivalent | No tokens | Manifest updated, counts reported in STATUS |
| 1. Triage (weekly, for new files) | Rules pass, then model pass on unclassified files; assign discipline and tier | `scripts/triage_rules.py`, then Haiku or the chosen classifier | Low | Every new unique file has a discipline and a tier |
| 2. Shortlist (weekly) | Tier A candidates grouped by discipline, at most 10 per sitting | Flint, labelled without the classifier | Low | Shortlist file in `docs/shortlists/` |
| 3. Approve | Eric approves, edits or rejects each candidate | **Eric** | Eric's time | Each candidate marked approved, edited or dropped |
| 4. Route | Papers go to Zotero. Books, decks and lectures go to the gate. Video and audio go to the transcription queue | Flint | Depends on route | Route recorded in the queue |
| 5. Gate (Tier A books and decks) | Atomize, independent review, fix, round 2 if needed, lint | Opus agents, one batch at a time | High (see section 4) | Staged entries pass the gate |
| 6. Promote | Dry run, then promote to the vault, after Eric approves the batch | `scripts/promote_to_vault.py` | Low | Vault commit; reciprocal links added |
| 7. Synthesis | One note per discipline, in the order in `docs/PLAN.md` Phase 4 | Opus, plus Eric's answers to the closing questions | High | Eric has answered the note's questions |

**Papers do not go through the atomizer.** A paper goes to Zotero (full text), then Flint searches Zotero. Only a book, deck or lecture is atomized. This keeps about 9,500 papers out of the most expensive stage.

## 4. Budget

**Cost of one gate batch.** Chapter 8 is 60 pages. The plan splits it into four batches. Each batch takes about five Opus calls: writer, independent reviewer, fixer, then a round-2 reviewer and round-2 fixer if the first review finds many problems. Chapter 9 is two sections, split into four batches. Eight batches is roughly 30 to 40 Opus calls, for about 130 pages. A rule of thumb for planning: **about 0.3 Opus calls per page**, plus a fixed cost of about two calls per batch.

**Capacity.** At a sustainable pace of one book-chapter batch a week, the gate can handle about 20 to 25 books in a year. That only works if the Tier A list stays short. The current Tier A list is 101 files from the model pass and a 97-file shortlist across 14 disciplines (approval pending). Most of that list is papers, which take the Zotero route, not the gate.

**Sub-agent limits.** Eric is usage-sensitive. The default cap is:
- At most one gate batch in progress at a time.
- No parallel fan-out of review agents.
- A weekly ceiling of about 15 Opus calls, to be confirmed by Eric. Above that, the next batch waits for the next week.

## 5. Cadence

- **Daily:** nothing automatic. Background transcription, if approved, runs overnight on the Mac.
- **Weekly (one sitting, about 20 minutes for Eric):** new-file triage output and a shortlist of up to 10 candidates. Eric approves or drops them. Approved Tier A items enter the queue in `docs/QUEUE.md`.
- **Monthly:** catalog delta run (stage 0). Counts updated in STATUS. Backlog size reported: promotion queue, unapproved shortlist, unrouted files.
- **Quarterly:** a backlog review. Drop any candidate that has sat unapproved for 90 days. Re-check the readiness check in `docs/flint-mobile-gaps-and-buildout-2026-10-12.md`.

## 6. Growth control

The Drive grows, so the plan cannot assume a fixed total. The rules that stop the queue from growing without limit:

1. New files enter the **catalog** automatically (stage 0). They do not enter the **queue** automatically. Only Eric's approval moves a file into the queue.
2. A cap on the open queue: at most 50 approved-but-unprocessed candidates. When the cap is reached, no new candidates are offered until the queue drops below 30.
3. Old unapproved candidates expire after 90 days, back to Tier B.

## 7. Sequence (what to do, in order)

0. **Recount** the catalog from the current Drive state. Reconcile the 62,072 and 17,847 figures. Report the true numbers in STATUS.
1. **Finish the gate for Supertraining Ch8 and Ch9** (in progress; brief at `staging/_gate_brief_supertraining_ch8-9.md`).
2. **Clear the promotion backlog** that remains from the Wave 1 and Issurin batches (already in the vault; confirm and close).
3. **Approve the 97-file shortlist** in sittings of 10 (Eric). This is the Tier A list. It replaces the open-ended queue.
4. **Route the shortlist:** papers to Zotero, books and decks to the gate, video to the transcription queue.
5. **Run the classifier comparison** (rules vs Haiku vs Jev, 200-file sample). This decides how the 4,009 unsorted files are triaged. Answer key first, blind.
6. **Set the weekly cadence** from section 5, once the recount is done.
7. **Start synthesis** for Rehab and return to play (the biggest gap in the baseline), once its shortlist items are in the vault.

## 8. What this plan does not do

- It does not ingest the whole Drive. Most of it stays catalogued and searchable by title only.
- It does not decide the classifier. Step 5 does that.
- It does not change any of Eric's approval rules. Promotion and shortlist approval stay manual.

## 9. Decisions for Eric

1. **Weekly sitting size.** Ten candidates a week (recommended), or five?
2. **Weekly Opus ceiling.** About 15 calls a week (recommended), or no ceiling?

He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Inference: the five groups below are this entry's grouping, not Siff's; the items inside them are his: movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; exercising of related muscle groups (principle 4); multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). # Field Sports: Do Not Let Endurance Work Undercut Strength and Power, and Bias Conditioning Toward the Short and Intermediate Energy Systems

**What it is** — Under "General Fitness Issues" the authors write: "It is vital to devise a programme in which training for one motor quality does not interact negatively with training for other fitness qualities. For instance, any unnecessary or prolonged emphasis on cardiovascular conditioning may decrease strength, hypertrophy and explosive power. In the individual workout, it is usually inappropriate to perform endurance activities before strength and speed training (Fig 1.7)" (PDF 438 / p.427, checked against the page image). On energy systems: recovery from bursts "may be facilitated in part by the cardiovascular and circulatory mechanisms of the *long term energy system*," but "most activity in sports played on a field relies predominantly on the short and intermediate term non-oxidative energy systems. The *short term* (ATP-CP) system provides energy for explosive bursts of activity lasting for no longer than 2 or 3 seconds, while the *intermediate* energy system is mainly involved with furnishing fuel for fairly intense activity of up to about 45 seconds (see 1.13)" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors give the interference effect as the reason: prolonged cardiovascular emphasis "may decrease strength, hypertrophy and explosive power" (PDF 438). They give no mechanism here and point back to Fig 1.7 and 1.13. Inference: endurance work first in a session leaves the athlete fatigued for the high-force, high-speed work that needs a fresh nervous system.

**When to apply** — Ordering a session (strength and speed before endurance) and setting the conditioning emphasis for field sports. After the energy-system choice, the authors turn to strength and speed: which fitness factors need training and "the main muscle groups which need strengthening in the different players"; "The introduction to more explosive training, especially plyometric methods, should be done cautiously and progressively, following the guidelines offered earlier (5.2.4)" (PDF 438 / p.427). Eric's review: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a 'worst case scenario' to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit). Inference: Eric and the authors agree on ATP-CP priority but differ on the other two systems. On the aerobic system, Eric programmes aerobic capacity/power as a primary goal (Goal 1), while the book subordinates it: field-sport activity relies "predominantly on the short and intermediate term non-oxidative energy systems," the long-term system gets only a recovery role, and "unnecessary or prolonged emphasis on cardiovascular conditioning may decrease strength, hypertrophy and explosive power" (PDF 438 / p.427). On the intermediate (glycolytic) system, the authors name it as a main field-sport system and Eric leaves it to practice. The book speaks of field sports in general and Eric of football, so this is a difference in emphasis and population, not a contested claim.

**When NOT to apply** — Endurance sports, where the long-term system is the target. The words "usually" and "may" are the authors' own hedges; there is no data on these pages. The time limits (2 or 3 s; about 45 s) are rough bands, not cut-offs. Inference: the authors say the long-term system aids recovery between bursts, so "less cardiovascular emphasis" does not mean none.

**Example** — The authors' session rule: in one workout, strength and speed training come before endurance activities, not after (PDF 438 / p.427).

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]], [[heuristic--depth-jump-weekly-frequency-and-seasonal-placement]]

Read first, in full: /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_gate_brief_supertraining_ch8-9.md (conventions, schema, review checklist, page convention PDF idx = printed + 11).

Scope:
- /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_scope_supertraining_ch8c.txt: the new entries come first (21), then a blank line, then the cross-linked existing entries (17). Review the cross-link additions too.
- /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/review_supertraining_ch8b_opus.md, for the failure modes found in 8b.

Source: PDF idx 467-477 (printed 456-466) of /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf. Extract the text with PyMuPDF. Render to /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_renders/ (names r8c_rev_p<idx>.png) and read the images for every number, table cell and figure. The text layer is OCR. The right and left margins are clipped on alternate pages in this range. Quotes that the writer marked "partly reconstructed" need extra care: check that the reconstruction is labelled and adds no words.

Checklist for each entry (from the brief): locator matches the page; numbers and quotes match the image; attribution is correct; labels present ("Inference:" for the writer's reasoning, "Eric's review:" with a baseline line number for Eric, checked against /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/docs/method-baseline.md); "When NOT to apply" is non-trivial; confidence fits the rule (full text allows proven at most; contested only for an internal contradiction, or a same-claim conflict in the same domain and population; supported entries need the named study described in the book); wikilinks resolve (FLINT_VAULT=/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain, and also check staging); no em dashes in the body; no athlete-identifying detail (the writer left out two named champions on PDF 469; confirm); heading format `**Label** —`.

Check the misprints the writer reported (Fig 8.7 called "Figure 3" on PDF 473; the "Psychological Stress" control factor without a definition on PDF 475; Fig 8.8 lettering on PDF 472 or nearby; Point E on Fig 8.9; the Shtanga grading on PDF 470). Confirm each entry that cites one says so correctly.

Check overlap with 8a, 8b and existing entries: an idea repeated without a cross-link is a FIX.

Give the missing-ideas count and the top three only.

Write the review to /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/review_supertraining_ch8c_opus.md with: header (reviewer, date 2026-10-13, source, pages read); verdict (GO, GO AFTER FIXES or NO-GO); a table with one row per entry (file, PASS / FIX / NO-GO, one-line reason); a numbered list of required fixes naming the exact file and sentence; the missing-ideas count and top three; a boundary note for 8d (8d starts at the 8.9 heading on PDF 478).

Return ONLY: verdict; counts of PASS, FIX and NO-GO for the 21 new entries and for the cross-linked files; the review file path; missing-ideas count. No entry text.

input.prompt:
You are the FIXER for gate batch 8c of Flint's ingest of Supertraining (6th ed.). Apply the reviewer's required fixes. Make no other changes.

1. Apply every required fix exactly as the review describes. Re-check each against the rendered images in /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_renders/ (names r8c_*.png). If an image you need is missing, render it with PyMuPDF at 150 dpi (220 dpi for figures) into the same folder.
2. Where a fix concerns a clipped margin or a partly reconstructed quote, keep the "partly reconstructed" label. Do not add words the image does not show.
3. Do NOT add the missing ideas. Record them only in your log.
4. Do NOT edit the vault at /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain. Do NOT promote. Do NOT edit _book.md unless a fix requires a row change, and then change only that row.
5. Keep the heading form `**Label** —`. No em dashes in the body.
6. Scope: the 17 new 9a entries in /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_scope_supertraining_ch9a.txt (lines before the blank line), and the cross-linked existing entries after the blank line, if a required fix names them.

3. Do NOT add missing ideas. Record them in your log only.
4. Do NOT edit the vault at /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain. Do NOT promote. Do NOT edit _book.md except to change the 9.1 part-a row if a fix requires it. Do not touch the 9 row.
5. Keep the heading form `**Label** —`. No em dashes in the body.
6. Write a log at /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/fixes_supertraining_ch9a_applied.md: header (fixer, 2026-10-13, review file); a table of file, change made, fix number; a section "Not applied: missing ideas, carried to coverage follow-up" listing ideas by name; and any fix you could not apply exactly as written, with the reason.
7. Run: cd /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint && FLINT_VAULT=/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain python3 scripts/lint_library.py strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky. Fix any issue in your files. Report any pre-existing issue in _book.md as pre-existing.

Return ONLY: fixes applied in full, in part and not applied (fix numbers); count of files changed; the log path; the lint result for your files. No entry text.
